```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                     fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
```

`evalpheno` constructs temperature-driven phenology models and fits them to
observed phenological dates. This example constructs a PhenoFlex model [@luedeling_phenoflex_2021],
adjusts its parameters, and fits its chill and heat requirements to two seasons.

The temperature data come from an experimental orchard near Bonn, Germany.
The phenology dates below are **synthetic teaching examples**. The short fit
illustrates the interface; it does not establish convergence or validate the model.

## Construct a model

`pheno_model()` constructs a PhenoFlex model by default, using the Dynamic Model
for chill and unscaled Growing Degree Hours (GDH) for heat accumulation:

```{r construct-model}
library(evalpheno)

phenoflex_model <- pheno_model()
phenoflex_model
```

## Adjust parameters

Supply a named vector to choose starting values. Parameters you omit keep
their defaults. Here, `yc` is the chill requirement and
`zc` is the effective heat requirement:

```{r adjust-parameters}
phenoflex_model <- pheno_model(parameters = c(yc = 40, zc = 250))
model_parameters(phenoflex_model)[c("yc", "zc")]
```

## Inspect the model

You visualize the submodels and the model structure with the `plot()` function.

```{r plot-model}
plot(phenoflex_model)
```

For the other structures, submodels, parameter units, and a table of available parameters, see
[Model structures and submodels](model-structures-and-submodels.html).


## Prepare weather and observations

The bundled daily weather covers 2007--2009. For the temperature data handling,
the [chillR package](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/chillR/index.html) [@luedelingChillRStatisticalMethods2024] is handy. 
The PhenoFlex model originates from the chillR package. 
Convert the temperature data to hourly temperatures
and create two seasons, each spanning August to June of the following year:

```{r weather}
data("cka_weather", package = "evalpheno")

hourly <- chillR::stack_hourly_temps(
  cka_weather, latitude = attr(cka_weather, "latitude")
)$hourtemps
years <- 2008:2009
seasons <- chillR::genSeasonList(hourly, mrange = c(8, 6), years = years)
names(seasons) <- as.character(years)

observed <- c(`2008` = 125, `2009` = 117)
```

Supply one observed day of the year per season, in the same order as `seasons`.
Here, the event is interpreted as bloom. Each weather season must contain
complete, consecutive days of hourly data with `Temp`, `Year`, and `JDay`
columns. If `Hour` is included, it must run from 0 to 23 for each day.


## Predict with the model

Pass the model to `predict_phenology()`. You can either pass a single seaon
or a season list.

```{r model-prediction}
predict_phenology(model = phenoflex_model, weather = seasons)
```

Predictions are days of the year with a fractional time of day, or `NA` if
the event is not reached. Under the package's date convention, `116.0` is
26 April at noon in a non-leap year. For seasons spanning two calendar years,
dates in the first year are relative to its end: `0` is 31 December at noon
and `-1` is 30 December at noon.

You can also vizualize the processes leading up the prediction with `plot_processes()`.

```{r plot-processes}
plot_processes(model = phenoflex_model, weather = seasons)
```


## Fit the model

Choose the parameters to fit by naming them in the bounds. Here, only `yc`
and `zc` are fitted; all other parameters keep their stored values.
`default_bounds()` suggests starting ranges, which you should review for
your species and data. This example narrows the heat requirement range:

```{r standard-fit}
bounds <- default_bounds(phenoflex_model, parameter_names = c("yc", "zc"))
bounds$lower["zc"] <- 180
bounds$upper["zc"] <- 350

fit <- fit_phenology(
  phenoflex_model, evaluation = phenology_rss,
  seasons = seasons, observed = observed,
  lower = bounds$lower, upper = bounds$upper,
  optimizer = "DEoptim", max_iterations = 2,
  control = list(NP = 20, trace = FALSE), seed = 17
)
fit$par[c("yc", "zc")]
fit$value
```

`phenology_rss` calculates the residual sum of squares between predicted and
observed dates. The optimizer minimizes this loss, returned as `fit$value`;
`fit$par` contains the fitted parameters. `seed` makes the search reproducible.

Two iterations keep this example quick. For a useful calibration, use more
observations, increase `max_iterations`, check convergence, and repeat the
search with different starting values or random seeds.
